posts.title: The niboshi returns for winter
posts.excerpt: When the mornings turn cold, the sardine bowl comes back to the card. What changes this year, and why it only appears in winter.
posts.content:
Every year, on the first morning cold enough to see your breath on Kaede-dori, the niboshi bowl goes back on the card. This year that was the second of October.

Niboshi are small sardines, boiled and dried in the sun. Simmered gently for two hours, they give a broth that is darker than our shoyu, a little bitter and very deep. Joined to the clear chicken and kombu broth, they make the bowl we look forward to most.

Why only in winter

Partly because the sardines are best when they are caught in late summer and dried through the autumn. Partly because a bitter bowl tastes right on a cold day and wrong on a hot one. And partly because a menu that never changes stops being noticed.

A bowl should taste of the week you eat it in.

Tomoe Hayase

The niboshi will stay until the plum trees flower, usually in early March. It comes with medium noodles, chashu, raw onion and nori.

posts.title: Eleven hours of broth
posts.excerpt: From five in the morning to four in the afternoon: what goes into the pot, when it comes out, and why it never boils.
posts.content:
The pot goes on at five. By the time anyone else arrives it has been moving quietly for two hours.

The morning

Whole chickens and a little pork bone go in first, with cold water filtered twice. As the water warms, grey foam rises; we skim it by hand for the first hour, until nothing more comes up.

At eight the kombu goes in, and comes out again at nine, before it turns slippery. At ten the aromatics: leek tops, a piece of ginger, a dried shiitake.

The rest of the day

From then on the pot only needs to be watched. It must never boil: a boil clouds the broth and makes it taste of the bones rather than the meat. On a good day you can read the bottom of the ladle through it.

At four in the afternoon the broth is strained and the pot is washed. Tomorrow it begins again.

posts.title: Noodles, cut at seven
posts.excerpt: Ren mixes flour and water before anyone else is awake. How the noodles for five bowls come from one dough, and why they rest overnight.
posts.content:
Ren Okabe starts the noodles the day before. Flour, water, a little salt and kansui are mixed, folded and wrapped, and left in the cold room overnight.

At seven the next morning the dough is rolled through the machine six times, rested for twenty minutes, and cut. Thin and straight for shoyu and shio; a little thicker for niboshi; thick and flat for tsukemen.

Why rest them

A rested dough is calmer: the water spreads evenly and the noodles cook the same from the outside to the middle. They are firmer in the broth, and they keep their spring longer.

By nine the noodles are portioned, one bundle for each bowl, and they wait in wooden trays until the noren goes up.

posts.title: How to sit at the counter
posts.excerpt: No tickets, no menus to wave over, no bookings. A short guide for your first visit to an eight-seat counter.
posts.content:
If you have never been to a counter this small, it can feel like walking into someone's kitchen. In a way you are. Here is what to expect.

  • Wait outside until the noren is pushed aside for you.
  • Take the stool you are shown; we seat people so that pairs can sit together.
  • Order from the card at your place. Tell us how firm you want your noodles.
  • Eat while it is hot. Slurping is welcome.
  • Pay at the counter when you leave, and say thank you to the cook if you like.

That is all. Nobody minds a first visit; most of our regulars still remember theirs.

posts.title: Closed for the August week
posts.excerpt: The noren stays down from the eleventh to the eighteenth of August. When we close, why, and what comes back with us.
posts.content:
Every summer we close for one week in August. This year the noren stays down from Tuesday the eleventh to Tuesday the eighteenth.

The pot is scrubbed and seasoned, the counter is sanded and oiled, and the cook goes home to the coast. When we open again on Wednesday the nineteenth, there will be a cold shio on the card for one week only.

Thank you for waiting.

posts.title: A season in the tare
posts.excerpt: The soy tare in the shoyu bowl rests for three months in a cedar barrel. A short note on what the tare is, and why it takes a season.
posts.content:
Tare is the seasoning at the bottom of every bowl, poured in before the broth. It decides whether the bowl is shoyu, shio or niboshi.

Our soy tare starts with two soy sauces from small brewers, a little mirin and dried scallop. It rests for three months in a cedar barrel in the cool room, where it softens and turns rounder.

The salt tare

The shio tare is quicker: sea salt dissolved in a little kombu stock with dried scallop and a splash of sake. It is made every week, and tastes best when the broth is young.
